```{r setup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
library(easystats)
library(patchwork)
mytheme <- function(sz = 30) {
  theme_gray(base_size = sz) + 
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
# Make mytheme the default rather than relying on every plot remembering
# `+ mytheme`. Plots built by other packages -- plot(), check_model(),
# ggeffects -- never get a manual `+ mytheme` and were rendering at
# ggplot's 11pt default, which reads as tiny next to the 40px slide text.
theme_set(mytheme())
# Seed here so chunks that inherit RNG state rather than seeding themselves
# are reproducible; without it those figures churn _freeze on every render.
set.seed(2021)
```


# Overview

## Assumptions Overview {.fs90}

- **Assumptions about the Formula**
    + Correct Functional Form
    + Perfectly Measured Predictors
    + No Collinearity/Multicollinearity

::: {.fragment}
- **Assumptions about the Residuals**
    + Constant Error Variance
    + Normality of Residuals
    + Independence of Residuals
    
:::


# Constant Error Variance

## Assumption {.fs90}

- For any value of $x$, the residual variance are constant
    + The spread of points around the line must be consistent
    + This is similar to Student's assumption of equal group variances
    
- This is also called "homoscedasticity" or "homogeneity of variance"
    + When violated, we say that there is "heteroscedasticity"

::: {.callout-important title="Consequences of Violating"}
Bias in standard errors only
:::


## Assumption Examples

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
set.seed(2021)
d1 <- tibble(
  x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100),
  y_met = 10 + 0.6*x + rnorm(100, 0, 0.5),
  y_violated = 10 + 0.6*x + c(rnorm(60, 0, 0.5), rnorm(40, 0, 2))
)
ggplot(d1, aes(x = x, y = y_met)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2, color = "darkgreen") + 
  mytheme()
```

:::
::: {.column}
```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=5, fig.height=5}
ggplot(d1, aes(x = x, y = y_violated)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2, color = "darkred") + 
  mytheme()
```

:::
:::

## Diagnostics

1. Breusch-Pagan heteroscedasticity test
    + A significant result indicates heteroscedasticity
    + But this test gets more power with a larger sample...
    
::: {.tc}
`check_heteroscedasticity(fit)`
:::

2. Plot the residuals against the fitted values
    + (Or some derivative of the residuals)

::: {.tc}
`check_model(fit, check = "homogeneity")`
:::


## Example: Assumption Met {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: false

fit_met <- lm(y_met ~ x, data = d1)
fit_violated <- lm(y_violated ~ x, data = d1)
```


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

library(easystats)
check_heteroscedasticity(fit_met)
```

::: {.fragment .pv2}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_met, check = "homogeneity")
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
#| message: false

see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_met, check = "homogeneity", panel = FALSE))$HOMOGENEITY + 
  mytheme(24) + 
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20)
  )
```
:::


## Example: Assumption Violated {.fs90}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

check_heteroscedasticity(fit_violated)
```

::: {.fragment .pv2}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_violated, check = "homogeneity")
```

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=5}
#| message: false

see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_violated, check = "homogeneity", panel = FALSE))$HOMOGENEITY + 
  mytheme(24) + 
  theme(
    plot.title.position = "plot",
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 22),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0, size = 20)
  )
```
:::


## Solutions

1. Transform the outcome variable
    + e.g., Log or power transformations

2. Adjust the standard errors
    + e.g., Huber-White (sandwich) estimation

2. Model the error variance explicitly
    + e.g., weighted least squares estimation
    + e.g., location-scale models


# Normal Residuals

## Assumption {.fs90}

- The residuals are normally distributed around the line
    + The spread around the line is a bell curve
    + This is more problematic with smaller samples
    + Non-normal residuals may signal other problems


::: {.callout-important title="Consequences of Violating"}
Standard errors will be biased
:::

## Examples

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
set.seed(2021)
n <- 200
d4 <- tibble(
  x = seq(0, 10, length.out = 100),
  y_met = 10 + 0.6*x + rnorm(100, 0, 0.5),
  s = sample(0:1, 100, TRUE, c(0.6, 0.4)),
  y_violated = (y_met - 8) * s
)
p1 <- ggplot(d4, aes(x = x, y = y_met)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkgreen") +
  mytheme(24)

p2 <- ggplot(d4, aes(x = x, y = y_violated)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkred") +
  mytheme(24)

(p1 | p2)
```

## Diagnostics {.fs90}

1. Plot the residuals' distribution
    + Visually compare density plot to normal distribution
    + Assumption is violated to the extent they differ

2. Use a quantile-quantile (QQ) plot
    + Visually compare the sample and normal quantiles
    + Assumption is violated if dots stray from the line

3. Use the Shapiro-Wilk test
    + A significant result indicates non-normality
    + But this test gets more power with a larger sample...
    

## Example: Residual Distribution {.fs90}

```{r}
fit_met <- lm(y_met ~ x, data = d4)
fit_violated <- lm(y_violated ~ x, data = d4)
```

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_met, 
            check = "normality")
```

:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_violated, 
            check = "normality")
```
:::
:::

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
p1 <- see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_met, check = "normality", panel = FALSE))$NORM + 
  mytheme(14)

p2 <- see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_violated, check = "normality", panel = FALSE))$NORM + 
  mytheme(14)

(p1 | p2)
```


## Example: QQ Plot {.fs90}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_met, 
            check = "qq")
```

:::
::: {.column}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

check_model(fit_violated, 
            check = "qq")
```
:::
:::

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.height=4}
p1 <- see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_met, check = "qq", panel = FALSE))$QQ + 
  mytheme(14)

p2 <- see:::plot.see_check_model(check_model(fit_violated, check = "qq", panel = FALSE))$QQ +

```


## Example: Shapiro-Wilk Test

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

check_normality(fit_met)

check_normality(fit_violated)
```


## Solutions {.fs90}

1. Transform your outcome to be more normal
    + e.g., Box-Cox transformations
    + e.g., Yeo-Johnson transformations

1. Use a nonparametric approach
    + e.g., nonparametric bootstrapping
    + e.g., rank-based nonparametrics
    
2. Model the outcome as non-normal
    + e.g., generalized linear modeling (GLM)
    
::: {.footer}
Note that addressing other issues may also help here.
:::

# Independent Residuals

## Assumption {.fs90}

- The residuals must be independent of (not related to) one another
    + This will be met in any random sample from a population
    + It will be *violated* with **clustered** or **autocorrelated** data
    + Clustered data has many observations from the same "group"
    + Autocorrelated data has many observations close in time

::: {.callout-important title="Consequences of Violating"}
Standard errors will be downwardly biased (i.e., deflated)
:::


## Example: Clustering

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
set.seed(2021)
n <- 200
d2a <- tibble(
  cluster_num = sample(1:6, n, TRUE),
  school = factor(fct_shuffle(factor(cluster_num)), labels = LETTERS[1:6]),
  x = rnorm(n, 0, 3),
  y_met = 10 - 0.4*x + rnorm(n, 0, 2),
  y_violated = 10 - 0.4*x + rnorm(n, cluster_num - 4, 1)
)
p1 <- ggplot(d2a, aes(x = x, y = y_met)) + 
  geom_point(aes(color = school, shape = school), size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkgreen") +
  mytheme(24)

p2 <- ggplot(d2a, aes(x = x, y = y_violated, )) +
  geom_point(aes(color = school, shape = school), size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkred") +
  mytheme(24)

(p1 | p2) + plot_layout(guides = "collect") & theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Example: Autocorrelation

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]
set.seed(2021)
d2b <- 
  read_csv("../../data/auto.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>  
  transmute(
    time = time, 
    x = employees, 
    y_met = sample(sales, size = length(sales)), 
    y_violated = sales
  )

p1 <- ggplot(d2b, aes(time, y_met)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2, color = "darkgreen") + 
  mytheme(24)

p2 <- ggplot(d2b, aes(time, y_violated)) + 
  geom_point(size = 2.5) + 
   geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 2, color = "darkred") + 
  mytheme(24)

(p1 | p2)
```


## Diagnostics

1. If there is a potential clustering variable, do residuals differ?
    + Examine distribution of residuals in each cluster
    + Calculate a multilevel intraclass correlation
    
2. Is there autocorrelation between residuals?
    + Use the Durbin-Watson serial dependency test
    + Significance indicates autocorrelation

::: {.tc}
`check_autocorrelation(fit)`
:::

## Example: No Clustering

```{r}
#| echo: false

fit_met1 <- lm(y_met ~ x, data = d2a)
fit_violated1 <- lm(y_violated ~ x, data = d2a)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
qplot(x = school, y = residuals(fit_met1), data = d2a, geom = "boxplot")
```

```{r}
qplot(x = school, y = residuals(fit_met1), data = d2a, geom = "boxplot") +
  mytheme(24)
```

## Example: Clustering

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
qplot(x = school, y = residuals(fit_violated1), data = d2a, geom = "boxplot")
```

```{r}
qplot(x = school, y = residuals(fit_violated1), data = d2a, geom = "boxplot") + 
  mytheme(24)
```


## Example: Autocorrelation

```{r}
#| echo: false

fit_met2 <- lm(y_met ~ x, data = d2b)
fit_violated2 <- lm(y_violated ~ x, data = d2b)
```

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

check_autocorrelation(fit_met2)

check_autocorrelation(fit_violated2)
```


## Solutions {.fs90}

1. Adjust the standard errors
    + e.g., cluster-robust standard errors

2. Model the clustering explicitly
    + e.g., fixed-effects modeling
    + e.g., multilevel modeling (MLM, HLM, LME, LMM)
    + e.g., generalized estimating equations (GEE)
    
3. Model the serial dependency
    + e.g., time series analysis (ARIMA)
    + e.g., autoregressive models (DSEM)


# Outliers

## Definition {.fs90}

- Outliers are **atypical observations** that do not fit the other data
    + They may represent data contaminated by errors
    + Or they may represent real but rare cases

::: {.fragment}
- Outliers can have **large impacts** on the results of your model
    + Results may reflect the outliers rather than general patterns

:::

::: {.fragment}
- So we need to be watchful for outliers and deal with them carefully
    + We should also be transparent about reporting our approach

:::


## Examples

```{r}
#| replace_path: ["../../data/", ""]
yearspubs <- read_csv("../../data/yearspubs.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```


::: {.columns}
::: {.column}

```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=3.5}
qplot(yrs_since, n_pubs, data = yearspubs, geom = "point") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "darkgreen") + 
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60)) + 
  mytheme(24)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
fit_without <- lm(n_pubs ~ yrs_since, data = yearspubs)
cof <- coef(fit_without)
```

$$b_0=`r round(cof[[1]], 1)`, b_1=`r round(cof[[2]], 1)`^\ast$$


:::
::: {.column .fragment}
```{r, fig.width=5, fig.height=3.5}
dat_with <- yearspubs
dat_with[2, 1] <- 66
qplot(yrs_since, n_pubs, data = dat_with, geom = "point") + 
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", linewidth = 1, color = "darkred") + 
  mytheme(20)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
fit_with <- lm(n_pubs ~ yrs_since, data = dat_with)
cof2 <- coef(fit_with)
```

$$b_0=`r round(cof2[[1]], 1)`^\ast, b_1= `r round(cof2[[2]], 1)`$$

:::
:::


## Diagnostics

For each observation, we can calculate its...

1. **Leverage:** How unusual are its $x$ values?
    + e.g., $h_{ii}$ and Mahalonabis distance
    
2. **Distance:** How far is it from the regression line?
    + e.g., raw, standardized, or Studentized residuals
    
3. **Influence:** How much does it change the coefficients?
    + e.g., $\text{DFFITS}_i$, $\text{DFBETAS}_i$, and Cook's $D_i$


## Example: No Outliers

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

check_outliers(fit_without, method = c("cook", "mahalanobis"))
```


## Example: With Outliers

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

check_outliers(fit_with, method = c("cook", "mahalanobis"))
```


## Solutions {.fs90}

1. **Fix** the outliers
    + If they are errors/contaminations, fix them
    
2. **Keep** the outliers
    + If they belong to your distribution, maybe keep them
    
3. **Remove** the outliers
    + If they belong to a different distribution, maybe remove them
    
4. **Recode** the outliers
    + If you want to reduce their influence, maybe Winsorize them
    
## Remove the Outliers

If you do choose to remove the outliers, here's how

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| collapse: true

# Number of observations before removing outliers
nrow(dat_with)

# Identify outliers
outliers <- check_outliers(fit_with, method = c("cook", "mahalanobis"))

# Remove outliers
dat_drop <- dat_with[!as.numeric(outliers), ]

# Number of observations after removing outliers
nrow(dat_drop)
```
